\frac{a^2}{4} + 2t &= b, \\

\end{align*}Similarly, if $x^4 + 2ax^3 + 2bx^2 + 2cx + 1$ is the square of a polynomial, then we can assume the polynomial is of the form $x^2 + ax + u.$  Hence,
\[x^4 + 2ax^3 + 2bx^2 + 2cx + 1 = (x^2 + ax + u)^2.\]Expanding, we get
\[x^4 + 2ax^3 + 2bx^2 + 2cx + 1 = x^4 + 2ax^3 + (a^2 + 2u) x^2 + 2aux + u^2.\]Matching coefficients, we get

2au &= 2c, \\
u^2 &= 1.

t^2 &= 1.

\begin{bmatrix}
a & b & c \\
d & e & f \\
g & h & i
\end{bmatrix}
\] is given by \(a(ei - fh) - b(di - fg) + c(dh - eg)\).

For the matrix
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & k & -1 \\
k & -1 & -1 \\
1 & 1 & -k
\end{bmatrix},
\]

\[1((-1)(-k) - (-1)(1)) - k((k)(-k) - (-1)(1)) + (-1)((k)(1) - (-1)(1))\]

\[= k + 1 + k^3 - k - k - 1\]
\[= k^3 - k.\]

The system has a non-trivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero, so we need to solve \(k(k^2 - 1) = 0\). This gives us the values \(k = 0, k = 1, k = -1\).

Therefore, the values of \(k\) for which the system has a non-trivial solution are \(\boxed{0, 1, -1}\).
